extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, writers and scholars interested in satire and satirical practice
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for creating and assessing satirical humour across genres and media, covering techniques, tone, targets, legal status, reception, and formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method and purpose of the satirist
rubrics_metrics.description: "I can set a braggart quailing with a quip, The upstart I can wither with a whim; He may wear a merry laugh upon his lip, But his laughter has an echo that is grim!"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire's purpose is to mock, expose, and humble targets (braggarts, upstarts) with wit that leaves a 'grim' echo — i.e., to reveal hypocrisy or vice through pointed ridicule. Use concise, cutting lines that undercut the subject; aim to produce enduring critical effect rather than mere frivolity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of satiric writing to treat social issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelists such as Charles Dickens often used passages of satiric writing in their treatment of social issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In longer fiction, insert satiric passages or episodes to illuminate and criticize social problems (poverty, policy failures, hypocrisy). Examples: Dickens' social critiques; Mark Twain's Huckleberry Finn inverting moral values to highlight societal wrongs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Juvenalian mode (bitter, biting satire)
rubrics_metrics.description: Osborne's satire was so bitter and biting that at one point he received a public censure from Parliament's then Home Secretary Sir James Graham. Osborne wrote mostly in the Juvenalian mode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Juvenalian satire is harsh, accusatory, and moralistic; it attacks perceived corruption or injustice with vitriol. Use when the aim is severe condemnation. Be aware this invites stronger backlash and potential censorship/prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reprising earlier satiric works / use of conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Literary satire is usually written out of earlier satiric works, reprising previous conventions, commonplaces, stance, situations and tones of voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draw on established satiric tropes and tones to position new work in a recognizable tradition. This can create resonance and layered meaning but risks cliché if overused; signal novelty or commentary on the tradition to avoid mere pastiche.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggeration (hyperbole) as a satirical technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Exaggeration is one of the most common satirical techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amplify traits, actions or policies beyond plausible bounds to reveal their absurdity. Use measurable extremes to dramatize critique (e.g., parodying marketing escalations). Avoid so extreme a distortion that the audience misses the target or reads it purely as fantasy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diminution as a satirical technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrarily, diminution is also a satirical technique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shrink or belittle the subject to expose weakness or triviality. Use understatement or minimization strategically (litotes, anti-climax). Balance with clarity so the minimization reads as critique rather than simple mockery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of caricature and parody (but not synonymous with satire)
rubrics_metrics.description: While satire often uses caricature and parody, by no means are all uses of these or other humorous devices satiric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ caricature/parody to simplify and expose key traits, but ensure the work has an evaluative or critical dimension (not just mimicry). Clarify intent or context when ambiguity could cause readers to interpret the piece as mere imitation rather than critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ridicule by taking statements to their furthest logical conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: The ridicule of the actions of politicians and other public figures by taking all their statements and purported beliefs to their furthest (supposedly) logical conclusion, thus revealing their perceived hypocrisy or absurdity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reductio ad absurdum: extrapolate a position or utterance to its extreme implications to expose contradictions. This method works well in political satire (e.g., Colbert-style persona). Be prepared for critics who conflate persona with the author's genuine stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish satirist from their persona
rubrics_metrics.description: Because it is essentially ironic or sarcastic, satire is often misunderstood. A typical misunderstanding is to confuse the satirist with their persona.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using an ironic persona, craft signals (tone, irony markers, framing) that indicate distance from the views expressed. Understand the anti-pattern: audiences who take the persona literally can embrace the parody's target positions, undermining the satire's intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess taste, timing and sensitivity (bad taste)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common uncomprehending responses to satire include revulsion (accusations of poor taste). In the weeks following 9/11 the American public at large found works of satire to be in bad taste and not appropriate for the social climate at the time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider audience sensitivity and social context before satirising topics closely tied to personal trauma (rape, cancer, recent tragedies). Timing matters: what is permissible or witty in one moment may be received as offensive in another. Expect variable reactions; weigh satirical benefit against potential harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target selection and risk of targeting the victim
rubrics_metrics.description: The character of Alf Garnett was created to poke fun at the kind of narrow-minded, racist, little Englander that Garnett represented. Instead, his character became a sort of anti-hero to people who actually agreed with his views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose targets carefully; satire aimed at bigotry or power can be co-opted by audiences who sympathize with the portrayed views. Avoid punches that primarily target already-marginalized victims; ensure the satirical frame makes clear who or what is being critiqued to reduce misinterpretation (examples: Till Death Us Do Part, All in the Family, The Chaser controversy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Degrees of biting / tone (venomous to mild)
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions of satire's biting effect on its target include 'venomous', 'cutting', 'stinging', vitriol. Because satire often combines anger and humor, it can be profoundly disturbing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide the appropriate degree of 'biting' for your goal: Horatian (gentler) vs Juvenalian (severer). Match intensity to purpose and audience tolerance. Stronger bite increases risk of backlash, censorship, or legal action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal protections and limits ('right to satire')
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire is protected by the constitution in Germany, Japan, and Italy. Since satire belongs to the realm of art and artistic expression, it benefits from broader lawfulness limits than mere freedom of information of journalistic kind. In some countries a specific 'right to satire' is recognized and its limits go beyond the 'right to report'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand local law: satire may enjoy special protections beyond ordinary journalism, but protections and limits vary by jurisdiction. Treat satirical use of public figures and symbols with awareness of defamation, impersonation or trademark laws (examples: The Juice Media controversy in Australia; proposed criminal code amendments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of censorship, prosecution and institutional pushback
rubrics_metrics.description: Because satire criticises in an ironic, essentially indirect way, it frequently escapes censorship... Periodically, however, it runs into serious opposition, and people in power who perceive themselves as attacked attempt to censor it or prosecute its practitioners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect potential censorship, bans, legal actions or institutional retaliation — historically (Archilophanes/Cleon, Bishops' Ban of 1599) and modern controversies (cartoon riots, TV show suspensions, lawsuits). Prepare mitigation (legal advice, disclaimers, distribution strategy) when targeting powerful institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire as a social movement tactic / strategic goal
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire is regularly used by social movements covering a range of issues to achieve strategic goals. 'Humour is essential to a successful tactician, for the most potent weapons known to [people] are satire and ridicule.' (Saul Alinsky)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use satire strategically to mobilize, delegitimize opponents, or diffuse tension. Align satirical messaging with movement goals; consider how humor affects persuasion and public opinion. Beware that strategic satire aimed at mobilisation can provoke countermeasures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical prophecy / predictive value
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire is occasionally prophetic: the jokes precede actual events. Examples include The Onion's satirical pieces presaging real policy actions, or Monty Python and The Simpsons referencing phenomena that later emerged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage exaggeration or speculative scenarios to illuminate trends; recognize that plausible absurdities can later appear prescient. This can increase impact but also invites literalist readings by audiences or critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formats and media for satire (news, TV, radio, web, games, literature)
rubrics_metrics.description: News satire appears in print, radio, television and the web (examples: The Onion, The Daily Show, Spitting Image, South Park, Monty Python). Satire features in novels, comic strips, video games and films.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the format that best suits satirical aims — long-form fiction for sustained social critique, sketch/TV for topical parody, news-parody for media critique, games for interactive satire. Each medium offers different freedoms and constraints (e.g., animation allows freer depiction of public figures).
